subject: 오르간과 교회 공간
title: An instrument built into the building
content: A pipe organ is not placed in a room; it is built for one. Its pipes are cut to lengths that suit the volume they will fill, its voicing is adjusted on site over weeks, and moving the instrument elsewhere requires rebuilding it. No other musical instrument is so bound to a single space. The architecture does half the work. A stone interior with a long reverberation sustains each chord after the player releases it, so the music written for such buildings uses slow harmonic change and lets sonorities overlap, while an instrument in a dry room requires a different style entirely. Composers knew which building they were writing for. The tradition of building organ cases as architecture reflects this. Pipes are arranged in symmetrical arrays framed by carved wood, so the instrument reads as part of the structure rather than as furniture, and its position — at the west end, in a gallery, beside the choir — determines how the sound arrives and where the player can see. Voicing is the craft that no drawing captures. A builder adjusts each pipe by hand once installed, listening in the room, altering the mouth and the wind supply until the note sits properly among its neighbours, and this work takes longer than the manufacture. Two organs built to identical specifications in different buildings will not sound alike. Restoration is therefore contested. An instrument altered over three centuries carries the tastes of each period, and choosing which state to restore means deciding which tradition to honour, since returning it to the original destroys later work that is itself historical. Every major project of this kind involves an argument that cannot be settled by evidence alone.

subject: 현악 사중주라는 형식
title: Four players and nowhere to hide
content: The string quartet occupies a peculiar position in musical culture. Composers have treated it as the form in which they say what they most mean, audiences regard it as demanding, and performers describe it as the hardest ensemble to play well. All three attitudes follow from the same structural fact. Four instruments of one family produce a homogeneous sound, so nothing is masked. A wind ensemble hides small errors behind differences of colour, and an orchestra hides them behind numbers, while in this arrangement each line is exposed and every deviation of tuning or timing is audible. Players describe a level of scrutiny that no other chamber music imposes. The four voices are close in range and function. Composers therefore cannot rely on contrast of timbre to separate the lines, and must achieve clarity through rhythm, register, and the shape of the material itself, which is precisely the discipline that makes the form attractive to them. Writing for it exposes weak invention that a richer palette would conceal. The tradition developed conventions that persist. Two violins, a viola, and a cello has remained fixed for two and a half centuries, while almost every other ensemble has changed, and works written for it are performed by groups that rehearse together for years because the coordination required cannot be assembled quickly. The aesthetic result is a form that rewards close listening and offers little to casual attention. Audiences unfamiliar with the tradition frequently find it austere, and those who follow it describe exactly that austerity as the point, since nothing decorative survives in a texture where everything is heard.

subject: 변주곡이 하는 일
title: Saying the same thing many ways
content: A set of variations states a theme and then presents it repeatedly transformed. The form appears in musical traditions across the world, and its persistence suggests it answers something basic about how listeners follow music: they need something to hold while everything around it changes. The theme supplies the constant. A listener who has heard it can track a variation by recognising what has been kept — a harmonic outline, a rhythmic shape, a melodic contour — and the pleasure lies in noticing the relationship rather than in the new material alone. Composers therefore choose themes that are simple enough to be remembered and interesting enough to survive repetition. Transformation proceeds along several axes. A variation may keep the harmony while replacing the melody, or keep the melody while altering the rhythm, or keep only the number of bars. The most ambitious sets move so far that the connection becomes a matter of structure rather than surface, and listeners describe losing and then recovering the theme, which is an effect the form alone produces. The order is composed rather than accidental. A well built set arranges variations so that difficulty accumulates, contrasts fall where attention needs them, and the final variation resolves what earlier ones opened, so the whole has a shape that no individual variation carries. The form has attracted composers precisely because its constraint is severe. Nothing may be introduced that is not derived from the theme, so invention must operate within a boundary the composer set at the beginning, and traditions from several cultures have used exactly this discipline to display what a musician can do with almost nothing.

subject: 진혼 음악의 관습
title: Music written for the dead
content: Compositions for funeral and memorial occasions form a tradition with unusually stable conventions. The texts are prescribed, the occasions are known, and composers writing such works inherit expectations that ordinary concert music does not carry, since an audience arrives already grieving. Restraint is the first convention. Music for these occasions avoids display, and passages that would demonstrate a composer's skill elsewhere are held back, because virtuosity draws attention to the maker at a moment when attention belongs elsewhere. Composers who ignored this were criticised sharply by contemporaries. Slow tempo and low register carry much of the effect. A descending line, a sustained low sonority, and a pulse near the pace of a slow walk are used across unrelated traditions, and the convergence suggests the associations are grounded in something other than any particular culture, though the specific forms differ entirely. The tradition also permits consolation. Many such works move from lament toward something calmer, and the shape of that movement is where composers differ most, since the question of what may honestly be offered to the grieving is not a musical question. Some works refuse consolation deliberately. Performance carries its own conventions. Applause is frequently withheld, the occasion is not framed as a concert, and audiences behave differently, which changes how the music lands. Works of this kind performed in ordinary concert halls are received differently from the same works performed at a memorial, and several composers have written about the discomfort of hearing their funeral music applauded.

subject: 가곡에서 시와 선율의 관계
title: Setting a poem to music
content: A song built on an existing poem faces a problem that a song written to a new text does not. The poem already has rhythm, emphasis, and shape, and the music must either follow those or override them, and either choice alters what the poem was. Following the words closely produces one kind of setting. The melody rises where the sense rises, pauses where the line breaks, and lets the natural stress of the language fall on strong beats, so a listener hears the poem intensified rather than transformed. Traditions valuing textual clarity developed exactly this approach, and their songs are frequently criticised for being musically plain. Overriding the words produces another. A composer may repeat a phrase the poet wrote once, dwell on a syllable, or set a whole stanza to a shape the poem does not suggest, and the result is a musical work that uses a poem as material. Poets have objected to this for as long as it has been done, and composers reply that the song is a new thing rather than a reading. The accompaniment complicates both. An instrumental part can comment on the text, contradict the singer, or supply what the words withhold, so the setting may say something the poem does not, and several celebrated songs depend entirely on this tension. Translation makes the problem visible. A song translated for singing must fit new words to a melody shaped by the original language, and the result frequently reveals how much the music had been following the sound of particular words rather than their meaning.

subject: 탱고의 이주와 변형
title: A dance that travelled and came back changed
content: Tango grew up in the port districts of two cities on one river mouth, among people newly arrived from several continents, and because no one tradition supplied it, its early form joined pieces from many. What happened to it afterwards shows how a popular art changes when it travels. Yet standing at home came late. The dance was tied to the poorest districts and to places that polite society kept away from, and the players who shaped it worked in exactly those rooms. Its first records were cut for an audience that its own country’s cultural leaders found embarrassing. Therefore export changed everything. Danced in European capitals before the First World War, it became fashionable among rich audiences, and because foreigners approved, its standing at home changed fast and it was reclassified as a national art. The sequence — dismissed locally, celebrated abroad, then embraced locally — has repeated with several popular traditions since. The form itself altered as it travelled. European audiences got a version with the frankness toned down and the steps tidied for ballrooms, and that version came back as a rival tradition, so the dance now lives in forms whose dancers eye each other with suspicion. The musical tradition developed separately from the danced one. Composers extended it into concert music, using the rhythmic patterns while abandoning any expectation that anybody would dance, and audiences for that music frequently know nothing of the ballroom form, which is a division that exists in several popular traditions that acquired an art music branch.

subject: 산조의 즉흥과 틀
title: Improvising inside a fixed order
content: A tradition of solo instrumental music in Korea presents a sequence of movements distinguished by rhythmic cycle, beginning slowly and accelerating through several stages to a rapid close. Within that fixed order the player improvises, and understanding how the two coexist explains a great deal about how such traditions transmit. The cycles are the frame. Each has a characteristic length, internal accent pattern, and associated mood, and a listener familiar with the tradition recognises the change and knows roughly where in the performance they are. A player cannot alter the sequence without producing something that the audience hears as a different form. Within a cycle the material is inherited rather than invented fresh. A performer holds a body of melodic patterns learned from a teacher, and a performance assembles and varies them, so what sounds like free invention is closer to fluent speech in a language absorbed over years. Different teaching lineages hold different bodies of material, and specialists identify a player's lineage by what they play. The drum is a participant. A single drummer follows the cycle, marks its structure, and calls out at points of tension, and the exchange between the two performers shapes how far the soloist extends a passage. No performance is timed in advance. Transmission remains personal. Students learn by imitation over years, notation is used only as an aid, and the tradition treats the relationship between teacher and student as the medium. Recordings have changed this somewhat, and practitioners disagree about whether learning from a recording preserves the art or freezes it.

subject: 이콘화가 지킨 규범
title: Painting where invention is not wanted
content: Icon painting operates under rules that most later European art abandoned. The subjects, their poses, the colours of their garments, and the arrangement of the composition are prescribed, and a painter who invents is not being creative but making an error. Understanding why requires setting aside the assumption that originality is the point. The image is understood as a likeness transmitted rather than composed. A painter copies from an established model, which was itself copied, and the chain is held to reach back to an authoritative original, so fidelity to the model is the whole of the painter's obligation. Manuals specifying proportions and colours were compiled and circulated for exactly this purpose. The technique reinforces the intention. Egg tempera applied in thin layers over a gold ground produces a surface that does not imitate ordinary space, and the perspective used frequently diverges from the natural kind so that the composition opens toward the viewer rather than receding. This is a deliberate refusal of the illusionism that other traditions pursued. Variation exists within the constraint and it is small. Specialists distinguish schools, regions, and centuries by handling, by the treatment of faces, and by minor compositional choices, and those differences are what the tradition permits. To an outsider the images look identical; to a trained eye they are as distinguishable as handwriting. The painters were mostly anonymous by intention. Signing would assert an authorship that the practice denies, and the discipline of the craft included fasting and prayer, so the whole activity was framed as service rather than as art in the sense the word later acquired.

subject: 수묵의 여백
title: The part of the painting left empty
content: In ink painting traditions of East Asia, unpainted paper is not background. It functions as mist, water, distance, or air, and the composition is organised so that emptiness carries as much weight as the marks, which is a use of blank space that European painting arrived at much later and by a different route. The convention is learnable and specific. A few strokes at the base of a sheet with nothing above them read as a mountain rising into cloud, and viewers within the tradition supply the mountain. The painter is not omitting something; they are placing marks so that the empty area acquires a character, and doing this badly produces a picture that looks unfinished rather than spacious. Ink behaves in ways that support the approach. A brush loaded with diluted ink on absorbent paper produces a mark that cannot be corrected, so the painter works quickly and decisively, and every stroke carries the record of its own making. Because correction is impossible, the discipline is in the preparation and the pause before the hand moves. The tradition connects this to a philosophy of restraint. Writings on painting from several periods argue that what is withheld does more than what is shown, and that a picture explaining everything leaves the viewer nothing, and painters were judged on economy as much as on skill. Calligraphy shares the same materials and the same values. The two arts were practised by the same people using the same brushes, and the ability to read a line as gesture transfers directly between them, which is why the tradition treats them as branches of one accomplishment.

subject: 실경 산수의 등장
title: Painting the mountain that is actually there
content: Landscape painting in East Asian traditions long worked from established models rather than from observation. A painter learned types of mountain, tree, and rock from a manual and assembled them, so a picture depicted a landscape in general rather than any particular place. A shift toward painting actual locations therefore represented a substantial change. The older practice had its own justification. A painting was understood to convey the character of nature rather than the appearance of one site, and copying from models transmitted the accumulated judgment of earlier painters about how a mountain should be rendered. Working from observation was regarded by some critics as a lower activity, closer to record than to art. The change came with travel and with a shift in what patrons wanted. Painters journeyed to specific mountains, sketched, and produced works identifiable by their subject, and viewers who had seen the place could recognise it. This introduced a new criterion of success that the older tradition did not contain. The technique adapted rather than being replaced. Painters continued to use inherited brush methods while applying them to observed forms, so the resulting works are neither copies of models nor studies from nature in the European sense, and specialists debate how far any given painting was made on site. Critical opinion divided at the time and remains divided. Defenders argued that painting from life restored honesty to a tradition that had become formulaic; opponents held that it reduced painting to description. The same argument has occurred in several traditions whenever direct observation was proposed as a corrective to inherited method.

subject: 책가도의 사물 배열
title: Shelves painted full of possessions
content: A genre of Korean painting depicts shelves crowded with books, scrolls, brushes, ceramics, and imported curiosities, arranged in a space constructed by a perspective that no single viewpoint could produce. The pictures were hung in studies and, in a period of considerable social change, they carried a specific meaning. Books dominate the arrangement. Stacks of bound volumes fill the shelves, and their prominence declares the owner's relation to learning, so the painting functions as a statement about what its owner values rather than as a record of what they possess. Several surviving examples were made for households that could not have owned the libraries depicted. The other objects record contact with a wider world. Ceramics, spectacles, clocks, and vessels of foreign origin appear regularly, and their presence dates the tradition and traces which goods were reaching the peninsula and were regarded as worth displaying. Art historians use these paintings as evidence for trade. The perspective is deliberately inconsistent. Individual shelves recede in different directions, so the eye moves through the picture rather than settling, and objects that would be hidden in a coherent space remain visible. This produces an image in which everything is displayed at once, which is what the genre required. The tradition eventually spread beyond the households that began it. Simpler versions were produced for wider markets, painted by unnamed artisans in quantity, and those examples show the same subjects handled more freely, which is the ordinary trajectory of a form that begins with an elite and moves outward.

subject: 단청의 색과 보호
title: Paint that decorates and preserves
content: The painted decoration on traditional East Asian wooden buildings serves two purposes that are usually treated separately. The patterns are ornamental and the coating is protective, and the tradition developed as a single craft addressing both, which explains features that look purely decorative. Timber exposed to weather decays. Mineral pigments bound in glue and applied over a prepared ground seal the surface against moisture and insects, and the thickness required for protection is greater than any decorative purpose would need, so the layering is functional. Buildings left unpainted in the same climate require replacement far sooner. The colours were determined by available minerals and by convention together. A limited palette dominates — a green, a deep red, a white, a blue, and black — and these correspond to pigments that were obtainable, stable in sunlight, and compatible with the binder. The symbolic scheme attached to the colours developed alongside their availability rather than dictating it. Patterns are applied through stencils. Designs are pricked onto paper, powder is pounced through the holes onto the timber, and painters fill the resulting outlines, which allows a large building to be decorated consistently by many hands. Surviving stencils are studied as documents of the craft. Repainting is periodic and contested. The coating must be renewed every few decades or the protection fails, and each renewal covers what was there, so almost no original work survives on buildings still in use. Conservators now debate whether to repaint as the tradition requires or to preserve historic layers, which sets the survival of the building against the survival of its surface.

subject: 화론이라는 글쓰기
title: Writing about how to paint
content: East Asian painting traditions produced an extensive body of writing about painting, composed largely by painters themselves, and this literature has no close equivalent in the European tradition before the modern period. Its concerns are worth examining because they differ from what later criticism assumed art writing should discuss. Much of it concerns the hand rather than the picture. Texts describe how the brush should be held, how the wrist should move, and what quality of line results, and they treat these as the substance of the art rather than as preliminary technique. A painting is discussed as a record of movement, so the writing about it is largely about how that movement should be made. Ranking systems appear early. Painters and works were graded into classes, with the highest reserved for work that appeared effortless and least constrained, and the criteria are stated explicitly enough that later readers can apply them. The valuing of apparent spontaneity above evident labour is consistent across many centuries of this literature. The writing is also prescriptive about character. Texts hold that a painting reveals the moral quality of its maker, so cultivating oneself is presented as part of learning to paint, and a technically accomplished work by somebody regarded as vulgar was ranked below a rougher work by somebody admired. This connection between ethics and aesthetics is asserted rather than argued. The literature functioned as training. Students read these texts alongside copying, so the vocabulary for discussing painting was absorbed with the practice, and a tradition in which painters, critics, and collectors were frequently the same people produced a criticism written from inside the craft.

subject: 표구가 그림에 하는 일
title: Mounting a painting is part of making it
content: A painting on paper or silk is not finished when the painter stops, although it may look so. It must be mounted — backed with additional layers, bordered with silk, and fitted for hanging — and the mounting determines how the work is seen, how it survives, and in several respects what it is. Its backing is structural. Thin paper or silk carrying wet ink will cockle and tear, so layers of paper are pasted behind it with a starch adhesive, and the number of layers, their weight, and the direction of their fibres all affect how the finished work hangs and how it responds to humidity. Therefore a poorly mounted painting distorts within a season. Its border is compositional. Silk of a chosen colour and width surrounds the image, and the proportions of that border alter the picture as decisively as a frame alters a painting, so mounters and owners select them with care. Because a work remounted with different borders reads differently, records of the original mounting matter to specialists. Format then determines viewing. A hanging scroll is displayed and then rolled away, so the work is seen periodically rather than continuously; a handscroll is unrolled section by section and read in sequence at a pace the viewer sets; an album is turned page by page. Each format implies a different relation between viewer and work. Remounting is a conservation necessity, although it is also a loss. Adhesives fail and backings must be replaced every century or two, which requires separating the painting from its supports — an operation that risks the work and that removes whatever the previous mounting recorded. The specialists who perform it train for many years.

subject: 병풍의 공간 분할
title: A painting that folds and stands
content: A folding screen is a painting, a piece of furniture, and an architectural element at once. It divides a room, blocks a draught, and carries an image across several panels, and its design must work as all three, which produces conventions unlike those governing a picture on a wall. The folding is compositional. Panels hinged alternately stand in a zigzag, so adjacent panels face slightly different directions and no viewer sees the whole surface flat. Painters accounted for this, arranging compositions so that the image reads from the angle at which the screen is used rather than from directly in front. Photographs of such works flattened for reproduction misrepresent them systematically. Continuity across panels is handled variously. Some works run a single landscape across all panels, accepting that the hinges interrupt it; others treat each panel separately, producing a sequence; and others group panels into scenes. The choice determines whether the screen is one picture or several, and traditions differ in which they prefer. The format suits certain subjects. A long horizontal composition — a river, a procession, a season passing — fits the proportions naturally, and the tradition accordingly developed subjects that extend laterally rather than compositions organised around a centre. A screen with a strong central focus fights its own shape. Function shaped survival. Screens were used, moved, and damaged, and many were eventually separated into individual panels and sold, so a great many surviving works are fragments of larger sets. Reuniting them is an ongoing project in several collections, and the evidence for what belonged together is frequently the mounting rather than the image.

subject: 유기 그릇의 제작
title: Vessels hammered from a hot alloy
content: Bronze tableware made by hammering rather than casting forms its own craft tradition, and this difference of method produces a different object. Cast vessels are shaped in a mould and finished by grinding; hammered vessels are formed from a disc of alloy worked hot, and the resulting metal has a denser structure that rings when struck. Its alloy is specific. A high proportion of tin makes the metal hard and gives the characteristic tone, and it also makes the material brittle at room temperature, so it must be worked while hot and quenched at the right moment. Workshops guard these proportions and this timing, since getting either wrong cracks the piece. The hammering itself requires a team. One person holds and turns the piece with tongs while others strike in sequence, and the rhythm of the blows must be maintained because a pause lets the metal cool below the working range. Observers describe this process as closer to a coordinated performance than to solitary craft. Its finishing determines the surface. The vessel is turned on a lathe or scraped by hand, then polished, and the degree of finish varies by intended use, since ceremonial pieces are polished to a mirror while working ware keeps the hammer marks. Both are traditional and they look entirely different. This craft nearly disappeared and was then revived. Industrial tableware in cheaper materials removed the market within a generation, the number of workshops fell to a handful, and national designation of individual practitioners has kept the technique alive. Recent interest in the antibacterial properties of the alloy has supplied a new commercial argument, which is the kind of accident that occasionally saves a craft.

subject: 한지의 쓰임
title: Paper used for everything except writing
content: A strong handmade paper produced from the inner bark of a shrub was used across East Asia for purposes that most cultures would not consider paper suitable for. Windows, doors, floors, clothing, and containers were made from it, and the range of uses reflects properties that ordinary paper does not have. Fibre length supplies the strength. The bark yields long fibres that interlock, so a thin sheet resists tearing far better than pulp paper of the same weight, and layering several sheets with adhesive produces a material stiff enough for boxes and light enough for screens. Objects made this way survive for centuries. Its behaviour with air and light suited architecture. Paper stretched over a wooden lattice admits diffuse light while blocking direct sun, and it passes water vapour, so a room enclosed this way does not accumulate damp. Buildings designed around this material treat the wall as a filter rather than a barrier, which is an architectural idea that glass does not permit. Treatment extends the uses. Coating with oil makes it water resistant enough for floor covering and for umbrellas; lacquering makes vessels; twisting strips and weaving them produces baskets and even furniture. Each treatment belongs to its own craft tradition with its own specialists. The making is seasonal and laborious. Bark is harvested in winter, steamed, stripped, boiled with ash, beaten, and formed sheet by sheet in cold water, and the number of workshops has fallen sharply as machine paper replaced it for ordinary use. What sustains the surviving makers is conservation work, since the material's durability makes it the preferred repair medium for historic documents worldwide.

subject: 짚풀 공예의 계절성
title: Making things from what the harvest left
content: Craft using straw and grasses is bound to the agricultural year in a way that few other traditions are. The material becomes available only after harvest, it must be selected and stored while still pliable, and the work is done in the months when field labour stops, so the calendar rather than any workshop determines the rhythm. Selection happens in the field. Stalks are chosen for length, straightness, and freedom from damage before threshing, since ordinary handling breaks them, and a household intending to make anything sets aside material at harvest rather than looking for it later. Once dried improperly the straw cannot be used. Moisture governs the work. Straw must be dampened to be bent and woven, and it stiffens as it dries, so the maker works within a window and rewets constantly, and objects are shaped while the material is soft and hold their form once dry. This is why the tradition produces rounded forms readily and flat rigid ones with difficulty. The objects were made for use and discarded. Baskets, mats, sandals, ropes, and containers were produced by households for themselves, replaced when they wore out, and returned to the ground, so almost nothing survives from before the modern period. What is known about older forms comes from depictions and from a small number of pieces preserved by accident. Ritual uses preserved some forms. Straw figures, ropes marking boundaries, and objects made for seasonal ceremonies continued to be produced according to fixed patterns after the practical objects had been replaced by manufactured goods, and those ceremonial forms are now the main surviving branch of the tradition.

subject: 청자 유약의 색
title: A green that took centuries to control
content: The pale green glaze on certain East Asian ceramics comes from a small quantity of iron in the coating, because it is fired in an air from which oxygen has largely been withdrawn. Small changes in any of those conditions produce a different colour, and controlling them reliably was the achievement that distinguished the great production centres. Yet the chemistry is unforgiving. Iron fired with oxygen present turns brown or yellow; the same iron fired in a reducing atmosphere turns green or blue-green, and the exact hue depends on the quantity of iron, the composition of the glaze, and the temperature curve. Therefore a whole kiln load could be lost by a change in the wind. Kiln design supplied the control instead. Long chambered kilns built on a slope draw air through the chambers in sequence, and the fuel and openings can be managed to starve the atmosphere at the right stage, so the architecture of the kiln is the instrument of the effect. Excavated kiln sites are studied for exactly this reason, although few survive intact. The valued appearance was specific and much argued about. Contemporary writings describe the desired colour with comparisons to jade and to the sky after rain, and collectors distinguished grades that modern analysis confirms correspond to measurable differences. The vocabulary of appreciation therefore came long before any grasp of the cause. Inlaid decoration developed as a further refinement. Designs were carved into the body, filled with white or black clay, and glazed over, so the pattern appears beneath a translucent green surface. Because this technique needed an extra firing and a body that would take the inlay without cracking, its mastery at particular workshops marks the height of the tradition.

subject: 분청의 자유로운 무늬
title: Pottery decorated quickly and without deference
content: A ceramic tradition that followed a period of highly controlled production took the opposite approach. Vessels were coated with white slip and decorated rapidly with brushed, stamped, incised, or scratched patterns, and the results are irregular in a way that the preceding tradition would have rejected. Speed shows in every mark. A pattern stamped repeatedly across a surface varies in depth and alignment, a brushed slip leaves the trace of the brush including where it ran short, and lines scratched through the coating are cut in one pass. Nothing is corrected, and the tradition's admirers regard exactly this as its quality. Production conditions explain part of the change. The centralised workshops that had made the earlier ware dispersed to regional kilns serving local markets, so vessels were made for use rather than for a court, at prices that permitted no elaborate finishing. What began as economy became a manner. Several techniques are specific to the tradition. Coating a vessel by dipping it and letting the slip run, brushing it on with a wide coarse brush so the strokes remain visible, and scraping away the background to leave a design in white are all methods that display the process rather than concealing it. Later admirers valued them precisely for that. The reception history is instructive. The ware was ordinary in its own time and became highly prized abroad, particularly in a neighbouring tradition of tea practice that valued irregularity, and some pieces were later returned to their country of origin as treasures. A domestic product judged unremarkable at home acquired its standing through foreign taste, which is a pattern that recurs in the history of craft.

subject: 처마가 만드는 그림자
title: Roofs designed to control light
content: The deep projecting eaves of traditional East Asian wooden buildings are usually described as protection from rain. They serve that purpose and they do something else that shaped the whole aesthetic of the interiors: they exclude direct sunlight in summer while admitting it in winter, and they produce a graded band of shadow that the architecture is composed around. The geometry does the work. The sun stands high in summer and low in winter, so an overhang of the right depth shades a wall when the sun is high and lets light reach far inside when it is low. Builders arrived at proportions empirically and the results correspond closely to what calculation recommends. Interiors are consequently dim. Light arrives reflected from the ground and from the underside of the eaves rather than directly, so the room is lit from below and from the sides, and surfaces within it were chosen for how they behave under that quality of light. Gold and lacquer read entirely differently in reflected illumination than under direct sun. A well known essay argued that the aesthetic of such interiors — the preference for muted surfaces, for depth of shadow, for objects that glimmer rather than shine — followed from this lighting rather than from any abstract taste. The argument is contested and it identifies a real relationship between the building and what was put inside it. Electric light dissolved the arrangement. A room lit evenly from above presents the same objects differently, and the traditional interiors now displayed in museums are frequently lit in ways that make them legible and destroy the effect they were designed to produce.

subject: 마루와 통풍
title: A raised wooden floor for a humid summer
content: Traditional houses in the warm humid regions of East Asia include a raised wooden platform, open on one or more sides, and this serves as living space in summer. Its construction answers the season directly, and because the same house usually contains a heated floor for winter, these two systems sit side by side in one architecture. Air moving underneath is its point. The platform stands clear of the ground on posts, so air passes below and the boards stay dry and cool, and a person sitting on them in summer is considerably more comfortable than on any surface in contact with the earth. That gap also protects the timber from damp and insects. Its boards are laid to permit movement. Wood swells in humidity, so planks are fitted into grooved beams without fastening, allowing each to expand and contract, and the small gaps that open in dry weather close when the air is damp. Therefore a floor nailed rigidly would buckle within a season. Openness completes this design. The space is bounded by columns rather than walls, with removable partitions that can be lifted out entirely, so in summer the house opens to the courtyard and air moves through. The same partitions close the space in cooler weather, which is why the room's identity changes across the year. These two systems in one house record a craft answer to opposite problems. A heated floor traps warmth and would be intolerable in summer; an open platform would be uninhabitable in winter, and the household migrates between them as the season turns, which is an arrangement that a single climate-controlled room replaced entirely.

subject: 정자의 자리 고르기
title: Choosing where to build a pavilion
content: A small open structure built for rest and view is among the most modest building types and among the most carefully sited. Its purpose is to be somewhere rather than to contain anything, so the choice of location is the whole design, and the traditions that produced such buildings developed elaborate reasoning about it. Water and elevation recur. Sites overlooking a stream, a pond, or a valley from slightly above are strongly preferred, since the position supplies a view, moving air, and the sound of water, and a pavilion at the same height as its subject offers considerably less. The preference is consistent across unconnected traditions. What is seen was composed. Builders selected positions so that particular features appeared framed by the columns, arranged plantings to conceal what should not be seen, and occasionally cut openings through vegetation to establish a view. The landscape was treated as material, so the building and its surroundings form one work rather than an object placed in a setting. The structure withholds as much as it offers. Walls are absent or minimal, the roof is generous, and the floor is raised, so the building supplies shelter and a defined place to sit while leaving the view unobstructed on every side. Anything more enclosed would defeat the purpose. Naming completes the design. Such buildings carry names describing what they are for or what is seen from them, frequently inscribed on a board fixed under the eaves, and poems composed there were sometimes carved on the columns. The building therefore accumulates a record of the responses it produced, which few other structures do.

subject: 가람 배치의 순서
title: Walking through a temple in the right order
content: A Buddhist temple complex is arranged so that a visitor passes through a sequence, and the sequence carries meaning that the individual buildings do not. Understanding the arrangement explains why such sites are laid out along an axis and why the approach is frequently long. Gates mark stages. A visitor passes through several in succession, each with its own guardian figures, and the passage from ordinary ground to sacred ground is divided into steps rather than crossed at once. The distance between them is deliberate, since walking supplies the time in which the transition occurs. Rising ground reinforces the sequence. Where the terrain permits, the buildings ascend, so the approach is an ascent and the principal hall stands highest, and complexes built on flat land achieve the same effect with platforms and stairs. The physical effort is part of the arrangement. The main hall sits at the end of the axis with a courtyard before it. That open space is where a crowd gathers, and its proportions relative to the hall determine how the building is seen on approach, which builders controlled carefully. A pagoda or a pair of them frequently stands in the courtyard, and their position relative to the hall varies by period and is used by historians to date a layout. Subsidiary buildings sit off the axis. Halls for particular figures, quarters for residents, and storage occupy the sides, so the central sequence remains uninterrupted, and a visitor following the axis encounters the intended order while those living there move differently. The plan therefore serves two populations with one arrangement.
